claim: Sleep is fundamental to the health and fitness of all animals.
source: Sleep is fundamental to the health and fitness of all animals.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus about sleep's importance.

claim: Following periods of sleep deprivation, individuals experience longer and more intense sleep bouts.
source: The physiological importance of sleep is underscored by the central role of homeostasis in determining sleep investment – following periods of sleep deprivation, individuals experience longer and more intense sleep bouts.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about homeostatic sleep regulation.

claim: Baboons sacrificed time spent sleeping when in less familiar locations, regardless of how long they had slept the prior night or how much they had physically exerted themselves the preceding day.
source: Baboons sacrificed time spent sleeping when in less familiar locations and when sleeping in proximity to more group-mates, regardless of how long they had slept the prior night or how much they had physically exerted themselves the preceding day.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Baboons sacrificed time spent sleeping when sleeping in proximity to more group-mates, regardless of how long they had slept the prior night or how much they had physically exerted themselves the preceding day.
source: Baboons sacrificed time spent sleeping when in less familiar locations and when sleeping in proximity to more group-mates, regardless of how long they had slept the prior night or how much they had physically exerted themselves the preceding day.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Baboons did not appear to compensate for lost sleep via more intense sleep bouts.
source: Further, they did not appear to compensate for lost sleep via more intense sleep bouts.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of sleep intensity.

claim: Baboons exhibited synchronized patterns of waking throughout the night, particularly with nearby group-mates.
source: We found that the collective dynamics characteristic of social animal groups persist into the sleep period, as baboons exhibited synchronized patterns of waking throughout the night, particularly with nearby group-mates.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of group sleep patterns.

claim: Every species, from honey bees to humans, allocates a portion of each day to sleep.
source: Sleep is an important and understudied facet of animal lives, with every species, from honey bees to humans, allocating a portion of each day to this period of rest (Cirelli and Tononi, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cirelli and Tononi, 2008.

claim: Sleep plays a central role in memory consolidation, support of the central nervous system, energy conservation, and physical restoration.
source: The universality of sleep reflects its central role in important physiological processes, including memory consolidation, support of the central nervous system, energy conservation, and physical restoration (Chowdhury and Shafer, 2020; Gangwisch, 2014; Stickgold, 2005; Vyazovskiy, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Failure to meet daily sleep demand has health consequences.
source: Accordingly, failure to meet daily sleep demand has health consequences (Basner et al., 2013), with potentially fatal repercussions of extreme sleep deprivation (Rechtschaffen and Bergmann, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Basner et al., 2013 and Rechtschaffen and Bergmann, 2002.

claim: Extreme sleep deprivation has potentially fatal repercussions.
source: Accordingly, failure to meet daily sleep demand has health consequences (Basner et al., 2013), with potentially fatal repercussions of extreme sleep deprivation (Rechtschaffen and Bergmann, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rechtschaffen and Bergmann, 2002.

claim: After periods of insufficient sleep or extreme physical exertion, individuals experience particularly long and intense bouts of sleep.
source: The physiological need for sleep is emphasized by its homeostatic control – after periods of insufficient sleep or extreme physical exertion, individuals experience particularly long and intense bouts of sleep (Kitamura et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kitamura et al., 2016.

claim: Homeostatic regulation has become an important criterion in the very definition of sleep.
source: Decades of sleep research have consistently implicated homeostasis as a primary determinant of sleep patterns, such that homeostatic regulation has become an important criterion in the very definition of sleep (Siegel, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Siegel, 2008.

claim: Laboratory and bedside sleep research has inherently overlooked the ecological pressures that drive the regulation and evolution of sleep.
source: A strong focus on studying sleep in the laboratory or at the bedside, although revealing much about the physiology of sleep, has inherently overlooked the ecological pressures that drive the regulation and evolution of sleep (Rattenborg et al., 2017; Reinhardt, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Rattenborg et al., 2017 and Reinhardt, 2020.

claim: Sleeping animals typically cannot engage in other behaviors that are important to their survival.
source: Sleeping animals typically cannot engage in other behaviors that are important to their survival (but see Lyamin et al., 2008; Lyamin et al., 2018; Rattenborg et al., 1999; Rattenborg et al., 2016), and investing in sleep when environmental forces render vigilance and activity particularly important may impose substantial costs to wild animals.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations, with exceptions noted.

claim: Sleep leaves animals in a state of extreme inattention, and thus highly vulnerable to their predators.
source: In addition to preventing animals from foraging, searching for mating opportunities, defending territories, and caring for young, sleep leaves animals in a state of extreme inattention, and thus highly vulnerable to their predators (Lima et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lima et al., 2005.

claim: The sentinel hypothesis suggests that staggering the timing of sleep bouts in a group can collectively maintain both high-quality sleep and high levels of antipredator vigilance.
source: Sleeping in a social context could alter the costs of sleep – the sentinel hypothesis suggests that staggering the timing of sleep bouts in a group can collectively maintain both high-quality sleep and high levels of antipredator vigilance (Samson et al., 2017; Snyder, 1966).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Samson et al., 2017 and Snyder, 1966.

claim: Cascading disruptions could lead to collective dynamics of sleep, such as the waves of wakefulness that have been documented in flocks of gulls.
source: Cascading disruptions could then lead to collective dynamics of sleep, such as the waves of wakefulness that have been documented in flocks of gulls (Beauchamp, 2009; Beauchamp, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Beauchamp, 2009 and Beauchamp, 2011.

claim: Baboons live in stable multi-male, multi-female groups of up to 100 individuals.
source: Baboons live in stable multi-male, multi-female groups of up to 100 individuals (Cheney and Seyfarth, 2008), and during the night, they seek safety in trees and rock outcroppings (Altmann and Altmann, 1970; Busse, 1980).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cheney and Seyfarth, 2008.

claim: During the night, baboons seek safety in trees and rock outcroppings.
source: Baboons live in stable multi-male, multi-female groups of up to 100 individuals (Cheney and Seyfarth, 2008), and during the night, they seek safety in trees and rock outcroppings (Altmann and Altmann, 1970; Busse, 1980).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Altmann and Altmann, 1970 and Busse, 1980.

claim: Leopard predation represents the single largest source of mortality for adult baboons.
source: Despite seeking refuge in these sleep sites, baboons remain particularly vulnerable to nighttime predation from leopards, which represents the single largest source of mortality for adult baboons (Cheney et al., 2004; Cowlishaw, 1994; Isbell et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cheney et al., 2004, Cowlishaw, 1994, and Isbell et al., 2018.

claim: Baboons' fitness depends heavily on their social relationships.
source: As a highly gregarious animal whose fitness depends heavily on their social relationships (Silk et al., 2009), baboons must also balance their time spent sleeping with their investment in social interactions as time constraints during the day limit their ability to build and maintain their relationships (Dunbar, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Silk et al., 2009.

claim: Time constraints during the day limit baboons' ability to build and maintain their relationships.
source: As a highly gregarious animal whose fitness depends heavily on their social relationships (Silk et al., 2009), baboons must also balance their time spent sleeping with their investment in social interactions as time constraints during the day limit their ability to build and maintain their relationships (Dunbar, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dunbar, 1992.

claim: Accelerometer-based sleep classification has shown an impressive ability to detect and monitor sleep behavior across taxa.
source: Accelerometer-based sleep classification has shown an impressive ability to detect and monitor sleep behavior across taxa (Ancoli-Israel et al., 2003; de Souza et al., 2003; Hoffmann et al., 2012; Ladha and Hoffman, 2018; Malungo et al., 2021; Qin et al., 2020), and is now commonly used to assess sleep in both humans (e.g., Jones et al., 2019; Patel et al., 2017) and nonhuman animals (e.g., Gravett et al., 2017; Reinhardt, 2020; Samson et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Validation studies comparing accelerometry to polysomnography generally show high accuracy (78–90%).
source: Validation studies comparing performance of this noninvasive method to polysomnography – the gold standard in sleep research – generally show high accuracy (78–90%; Ancoli-Israel et al., 2003; Kanady et al., 2011; Malungo et al., 2021; Shambroom et al., 2012), although concerns remain about the ability of movement-based methods to distinguish sleep from resting wakefulness (Ancoli-Israel et al., 2003; de Souza et al., 2003), and results must be evaluated with these caveats in mind.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Concerns remain about the ability of movement-based methods to distinguish sleep from resting wakefulness.
source: Validation studies comparing performance of this noninvasive method to polysomnography – the gold standard in sleep research – generally show high accuracy (78–90%; Ancoli-Israel et al., 2003; Kanady et al., 2011; Malungo et al., 2021; Shambroom et al., 2012), although concerns remain about the ability of movement-based methods to distinguish sleep from resting wakefulness (Ancoli-Israel et al., 2003; de Souza et al., 2003), and results must be evaluated with these caveats in mind.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ancoli-Israel et al., 2003 and de Souza et al., 2003.

claim: The diel pattern of activity in wild baboons reveals a clear monophasic sleep pattern, with individuals active during the day and inactive at night.
source: The diel pattern of activity in wild baboons, as reflected by accelerometry data, reveals a clear monophasic sleep pattern, with individuals active during the day and inactive at night (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Sleep onset occurred 53.0 ± 1.7 (mean ± SE) min prior to the end of evening astronomical twilight.
source: Sleep onset occurred 53.0 ± 1.7 (mean ± SE) min prior to the end of evening astronomical twilight, and baboons awoke 35.9 ± 1.7 min after the beginning of morning astronomical twilight (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Baboons awoke 35.9 ± 1.7 min after the beginning of morning astronomical twilight.
source: Sleep onset occurred 53.0 ± 1.7 (mean ± SE) min prior to the end of evening astronomical twilight, and baboons awoke 35.9 ± 1.7 min after the beginning of morning astronomical twilight (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The duration of the sleep period was 11.0 ± 0.04 hr on average.
source: The duration of the sleep period – the period between sleep onset and awakening – was 11.0 ± 0.04 hr on average.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Within the sleep period, baboons slept for an average of 9.2 ± 0.04 hr (total sleep time).
source: Within the sleep period, baboons slept for an average of 9.2 ± 0.04 hr (total sleep time), displaying an average sleep efficiency of 85.0% ± 0.2%.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Baboons displayed an average sleep efficiency of 85.0% ± 0.2%.
source: Within the sleep period, baboons slept for an average of 9.2 ± 0.04 hr (total sleep time), displaying an average sleep efficiency of 85.0% ± 0.2%.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Baboons exhibited 1.8 ± 0.03 distinct wake bouts per hour of sleep during the sleep period (sleep fragmentation).
source: Baboons exhibited 1.8 ± 0.03 distinct wake bouts per hour of sleep during the sleep period (sleep fragmentation).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Males slept an average of 20 min longer than females.
source: Males slept an average of 20 min longer than females and experienced 0.23 fewer wake bouts per hour of sleep (total sleep time linear mixed model [LMM]: standardized estimate [95% credible interval lower bound, 95% credible interval upper bound]: 0.44 [–0.05, 0.94]; sleep fragmentation LMM: –0.44 [–1.04, 0.17]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: Males experienced 0.23 fewer wake bouts per hour of sleep than females.
source: Males slept an average of 20 min longer than females and experienced 0.23 fewer wake bouts per hour of sleep (total sleep time linear mixed model [LMM]: standardized estimate [95% credible interval lower bound, 95% credible interval upper bound]: 0.44 [–0.05, 0.94]; sleep fragmentation LMM: –0.44 [–1.04, 0.17]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: Juveniles and subadults slept, on average, 16 min less than adults.
source: Juveniles and subadults slept, on average, 16 min less and woke on 0.38 and 0.28 more occasions per hour of sleep, respectively, than adults (total sleep time LMM: juveniles: –0.34 [–1.15, 0.50], subadults: –0.34 [–0.81, 0.14]; sleep fragmentation LMM: juveniles: 0.72 [–0.28, 1.75], subadults: 0.52 [–0.06, 1.10]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: Juveniles woke on 0.38 more occasions per hour of sleep than adults.
source: Juveniles and subadults slept, on average, 16 min less and woke on 0.38 and 0.28 more occasions per hour of sleep, respectively, than adults (total sleep time LMM: juveniles: –0.34 [–1.15, 0.50], subadults: –0.34 [–0.81, 0.14]; sleep fragmentation LMM: juveniles: 0.72 [–0.28, 1.75], subadults: 0.52 [–0.06, 1.10]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: Subadults woke on 0.28 more occasions per hour of sleep than adults.
source: Juveniles and subadults slept, on average, 16 min less and woke on 0.38 and 0.28 more occasions per hour of sleep, respectively, than adults (total sleep time LMM: juveniles: –0.34 [–1.15, 0.50], subadults: –0.34 [–0.81, 0.14]; sleep fragmentation LMM: juveniles: 0.72 [–0.28, 1.75], subadults: 0.52 [–0.06, 1.10]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: Neither total sleep time nor sleep fragmentation the previous night affected time spent napping the following day.
source: Neither total sleep time nor sleep fragmentation the previous night affected time spent napping the following day, time spent sleeping the following night, or the fragmentation of sleep the following night (Supplementary file 1f; time spent napping LMM: previous night total sleep time: 0.03 [–0.10, 0.17], previous night sleep fragmentation: 0.00 [–0.11, 0.12]; Figure 2A i-ii, total sleep time LMM: previous night relative total sleep time: –0.04 [–0.19, 0.12], previous night relative sleep fragmentation: –0.06 [–0.19, 0.06]; Figure 2B i-ii, sleep fragmentation LMM: previous night relative total sleep time: 0.09 [–0.10, 0.27], previous night relative sleep fragmentation: –0.03 [–0.18, 0.12]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: After spending more time napping during the day, baboons experienced shorter total sleep time during the night.
source: However, after spending more time napping during the day, baboons did experience shorter total sleep time and more fragmented sleep during the night (Figure 2Ai and Bi; total sleep time LMM: –0.19 [–0.36, –0.01], sleep fragmentation LMM: 0.22 [0.00, 0.45]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: After spending more time napping during the day, baboons experienced more fragmented sleep during the night.
source: However, after spending more time napping during the day, baboons did experience shorter total sleep time and more fragmented sleep during the night (Figure 2Ai and Bi; total sleep time LMM: –0.19 [–0.36, –0.01], sleep fragmentation LMM: 0.22 [0.00, 0.45]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: For every 10 min spent napping, baboons spent six fewer minutes sleeping the following night and woke 0.10 times more per hour of sleep.
source: For every 10 min spent napping, baboons spent six fewer minutes sleeping the following night and woke 0.10 times more per hour of sleep.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: Neither sleep duration nor fragmentation was influenced by the distance baboons traveled.
source: Neither sleep duration nor fragmentation was influenced by the distance baboons traveled (Figure 2Aiv and Biv; total sleep time LMM: –0.03 [–0.19, 0.14]; sleep fragmentation LMM: –0.04 [–0.13, 0.05]) or the VeDBA they accumulated during the day (Supplementary file 1e; Supplementary file 1l total sleep time LMM: –0.12 [–0.34, 0.12]; sleep fragmentation LMM: –0.05 [–0.33, 0.23]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: Neither sleep duration nor fragmentation was influenced by the VeDBA baboons accumulated during the day.
source: Neither sleep duration nor fragmentation was influenced by the distance baboons traveled (Figure 2Aiv and Biv; total sleep time LMM: –0.03 [–0.19, 0.14]; sleep fragmentation LMM: –0.04 [–0.13, 0.05]) or the VeDBA they accumulated during the day (Supplementary file 1e; Supplementary file 1l total sleep time LMM: –0.12 [–0.34, 0.12]; sleep fragmentation LMM: –0.05 [–0.33, 0.23]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: In humans, homeostatic regulation of sleep manifests within as well as between nights: sleep wanes and wakeful activity increases over the course of the sleep period as individuals gradually fulfill their sleep requirements.
source: In humans, homeostatic regulation of sleep manifests within as well as between nights: sleep wanes and wakeful activity increases over the course of the sleep period as individuals gradually fulfill their sleep requirements (Winnebeck et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Winnebeck et al., 2018.

claim: Baboons' probability of being asleep did not decrease as the night progressed despite exhibiting cyclic sleep patterns that are otherwise similar to patterns of human sleep.
source: Baboons, in contrast, did not demonstrate this pattern: their probability of being asleep did not decrease as the night progressed despite exhibiting cyclic sleep patterns that are otherwise similar to patterns of human sleep (Figure 2C; generalized additive mixed model [GAMM]: r2adj = 0.008, F(8.741) = 89.16, p<1 × 10–15).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: For the first 21 nights of the study, group members slept at the same site along the Ewaso Ng'iro river, distributed across 10 adjacent yellow fever (Vachellia xanthophloea) trees.
source: For the first 21 nights of the study, group members slept at the same site along the Ewaso Ng'iro river, distributed across 10 adjacent yellow fever (Vachellia xanthophloea) trees (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a description of the study observations.

claim: Individuals showed high fidelity to particular sleep trees.
source: Individuals showed high fidelity to particular sleep trees (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; one-tailed two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test: p<1.0 × 10–9), returning each night to one of the small set of available trees populated by the group.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: The choice of tree itself influenced sleep duration.
source: Not only did the choice of tree itself influence sleep duration (Supplementary file 1c, d, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), but the individual's familiarity with their selected tree impacted how much they slept.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: Baboons slept longer in trees to which they showed higher fidelity.
source: Baboons slept longer in trees to which they showed higher fidelity (Figure 3C; LMM: 0.21 [0.05, 0.36]), with individuals sleeping up to 33.4 min longer in the tree to which they showed highest fidelity than in the tree to which they showed lowest fidelity.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: Individuals slept up to 33.4 min longer in the tree to which they showed highest fidelity than in the tree to which they showed lowest fidelity.
source: Baboons slept longer in trees to which they showed higher fidelity (Figure 3C; LMM: 0.21 [0.05, 0.36]), with individuals sleeping up to 33.4 min longer in the tree to which they showed highest fidelity than in the tree to which they showed lowest fidelity.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: Baboons did not compensate for shorter sleep duration with less fragmented sleep when sleeping in nonpreferred trees.
source: Baboons did not compensate for shorter sleep duration with less fragmented sleep when sleeping in nonpreferred trees (LMM: –0.05 [–0.24, 0.14]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: At 20:55 on the 21st night of the study, a leopard mounted an unsuccessful attack on the group in their sleep site.
source: At 20:55 on the 21st night of the study, a leopard mounted an unsuccessful attack on the group in their sleep site.
evidence: This is a description of an observed event during the study.

claim: The day following the leopard attack, the baboons moved to a new sleep site 1.5 km away from their main sleep site.
source: On the day following this attack, the group moved to a less commonly used sleep site 1.5 km away (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a description of observed behavior following the leopard attack.

claim: Baboons slept 72 min less upon moving to the less familiar sleep site.
source: While the baboons showed no substantial change in their sleep duration or fragmentation on the night of the leopard attack (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4; total sleep time LMM: –0.25 [–0.87, 0.39]; sleep fragmentation LMM: –0.32 [–0.96, 0.33]), they slept 72 min less and exhibited 0.50 more wake bouts per hour of sleep, on average, upon moving to the less familiar sleep site (Figure 3D, total sleep time LMM: –1.52 [–2.15, –0.86]; sleep fragmentation LMM 0.96 [0.33, 1.60]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: Baboons exhibited 0.50 more wake bouts per hour of sleep upon moving to the less familiar sleep site.
source: While the baboons showed no substantial change in their sleep duration or fragmentation on the night of the leopard attack (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4; total sleep time LMM: –0.25 [–0.87, 0.39]; sleep fragmentation LMM: –0.32 [–0.96, 0.33]), they slept 72 min less and exhibited 0.50 more wake bouts per hour of sleep, on average, upon moving to the less familiar sleep site (Figure 3D, total sleep time LMM: –1.52 [–2.15, –0.86]; sleep fragmentation LMM 0.96 [0.33, 1.60]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: The decrease in total sleep time and increase in fragmentation following the change in sites was limited to the first night in the new sleep site.
source: This decrease in total sleep time and increase in fragmentation following the change in sites was limited to the first night in the new sleep site, after which sleep duration and fragmentation returned to normal (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The proportion of the night in which at least one individual was awake was significantly less than expected by chance.
source: Contrary to predictions of the sentinel hypothesis, the proportion of the night in which at least one individual was awake was significantly less than expected by chance (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Fisher's exact test: p<0.0001; Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, Fisher's exact test: p<0.0001), suggesting that, rather than staggering periods of nocturnal wakefulness, group-mates were actually synchronized in their sleep-wake patterns throughout the night.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: A significantly greater proportion of the group exhibited the same simultaneous behavior, either being asleep or awake, than expected.
source: Confirming this synchronization, we found that a significantly greater proportion of the group exhibited the same simultaneous behavior, either being asleep or awake, than expected (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Fisher's exact test: p<0.0001; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, Fisher's exact test: p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: Pairs of baboons showed more synchronization when sleeping in the same tree than when sleeping in different trees.
source: Moreover, pairs of baboons showed more synchronization when sleeping in the same tree than when sleeping in different trees (Figure 4C; LMM: 0.56 [0.47, 0.64]), which suggested that sleeping individuals may awaken in response to the activity of group-mates in their local environment, or that external disruptions in the local environment may simultaneously waken all group members in the vicinity.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: Individuals slept less when sharing their sleeping tree with more group-mates.
source: To distinguish between these potential explanations, we tested the influence of the number of group-mates in an individual's local environment on their total sleep time and found that individuals slept less when sharing their sleeping tree with more group-mates (Figure 4D; LMM: –0.53 [–0.87, –0.19]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: Each additional tracked group-mate in a tree resulted in a 4.0 min decrease in total sleep time.
source: Each additional tracked group-mate in a tree resulted in a 4.0 min decrease in total sleep time.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: Individuals were substantially more likely to wake following the awakening of others in their sleep tree.
source: We found that although individuals were indeed substantially more likely to wake following the awakening of others in their sleep tree, neither shorter duration nor more fragmented sleep the previous night dampened their responsiveness to group-mates (Bernoulli generalized linear mixed model [GLMM]: influence of group-mate activity: 0.25 [0.16, 0.34], interaction between influence of group-mate activity and previous night relative total sleep time: –0.01 [ –0.13, 0.10], interaction between influence of group-mate activity and previous night relative sleep fragmentation: –0.01 [ –0.11, 0.09]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: Neither shorter duration nor more fragmented sleep the previous night dampened baboons' responsiveness to group-mates.
source: We found that although individuals were indeed substantially more likely to wake following the awakening of others in their sleep tree, neither shorter duration nor more fragmented sleep the previous night dampened their responsiveness to group-mates (Bernoulli generalized linear mixed model [GLMM]: influence of group-mate activity: 0.25 [0.16, 0.34], interaction between influence of group-mate activity and previous night relative total sleep time: –0.01 [ –0.13, 0.10], interaction between influence of group-mate activity and previous night relative sleep fragmentation: –0.01 [ –0.11, 0.09]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: There was no influence of moon phase on baboon sleep duration or fragmentation.
source: We found no influence of moon phase or the minimum ambient temperature during the night on baboon sleep duration or fragmentation (total sleep time LMM: moon phase: 0.05 [–0.12, 0.22], temperature: –0.04 [–0.20, 0.13]; sleep fragmentation LMM: moon phase: –0.08 [–0.30, 0.13], temperature: 0.04 [–0.17, 0.26]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: There was no influence of minimum ambient temperature during the night on baboon sleep duration or fragmentation.
source: We found no influence of moon phase or the minimum ambient temperature during the night on baboon sleep duration or fragmentation (total sleep time LMM: moon phase: 0.05 [–0.12, 0.22], temperature: –0.04 [–0.20, 0.13]; sleep fragmentation LMM: moon phase: –0.08 [–0.30, 0.13], temperature: 0.04 [–0.17, 0.26]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: Baboons are highly vulnerable to nocturnal predation.
source: We show that, while baboons sleep less in unfamiliar environments, and while their sleep is disrupted by the activity of group-mates, their recent history of sleep and physical exertion has only a limited role in influencing sleep behavior. Because baboons are highly vulnerable to nocturnal predation (Busse, 1980; Cheney et al., 2004; Isbell et al., 2018) and because they experience fitness benefits from maintaining strong social bonds (Silk et al., 2009), sacrificing sleep to maintain alertness in novel environments and to remain close to group-mates may represent critical adaptations.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Busse, 1980, Cheney et al., 2004, and Isbell et al., 2018.

claim: Baboons experience fitness benefits from maintaining strong social bonds.
source: We show that, while baboons sleep less in unfamiliar environments, and while their sleep is disrupted by the activity of group-mates, their recent history of sleep and physical exertion has only a limited role in influencing sleep behavior. Because baboons are highly vulnerable to nocturnal predation (Busse, 1980; Cheney et al., 2004; Isbell et al., 2018) and because they experience fitness benefits from maintaining strong social bonds (Silk et al., 2009), sacrificing sleep to maintain alertness in novel environments and to remain close to group-mates may represent critical adaptations.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Silk et al., 2009.

claim: Sacrificing sleep to maintain alertness in novel environments and to remain close to group-mates may represent critical adaptations for baboons.
source: Because baboons are highly vulnerable to nocturnal predation (Busse, 1980; Cheney et al., 2004; Isbell et al., 2018) and because they experience fitness benefits from maintaining strong social bonds (Silk et al., 2009), sacrificing sleep to maintain alertness in novel environments and to remain close to group-mates may represent critical adaptations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in light of cited literature.

claim: Decades of research in the laboratory and at the bedside have implicated homeostatic regulation as a key driver of sleep patterns.
source: Decades of research in the laboratory and at the bedside have implicated homeostatic regulation as a key driver of sleep patterns, with the sleep rebound that follows periods of deficit facilitating the maintenance of a physiologically required amount of sleep (Amlaner et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Amlaner et al., 2009.

claim: In the natural world, 'sleep need' may be a relatively flexible concept, with variation in sleep investment driven as much by the opportunity costs of sleep as by its physiological benefits.
source: Our findings suggest that, in the natural world, 'sleep need' may be a relatively flexible concept, with variation in sleep investment driven as much by the opportunity costs of sleep as by its physiological benefits.
evidence: This is an interpretation and inference from the study's findings.

claim: Sleeping animals are highly vulnerable to predation.
source: There are substantial opportunity costs of devoting a significant portion of every day to sleeping. Sleeping animals are highly vulnerable to predation (Lima et al., 2005), and our results suggest that individuals sleep less when the risk of predation is particularly high.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lima et al., 2005.

claim: Predation risk tends to be greater in unfamiliar locations.
source: Given that predation risk tends to be greater in unfamiliar locations (Forrester et al., 2015; Gehr et al., 2020; Yoder et al., 2004), baboons appear to trade sleep for vigilance according to the current risk of predation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Forrester et al., 2015, Gehr et al., 2020, and Yoder et al., 2004.

claim: Leopards, as stealth hunters, are disinclined to launch repeated attacks.
source: This surprising result may reflect leopards' disinclination, as stealth hunters, to launch repeated attacks (Hayward et al., 2006; Lin et al., 2020), or indicate that baboons perceive uncertainty in the level of risk as potentially more dangerous than a confirmed threat.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Hayward et al., 2006 and Lin et al., 2020.

claim: Animals forego sleep when ecological demands increase the associated opportunity costs.
source: Consistent with our results, recent studies in ecologically relevant contexts have revealed that animals forego sleep when ecological demands increase the associated opportunity costs.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by subsequent examples and citations.

claim: Great frigatebirds reduced the amount they slept by 92.7% while engaging in long, nonstop flights, without apparent physiological consequences.
source: For example, while engaging in long, nonstop flights, great frigatebirds reduced the amount they slept by 92.7%, without apparent physiological consequences (Rattenborg et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rattenborg et al., 2016.

claim: Male pectoral sandpipers greatly reduce their time spent sleeping during their short and intense mating season, and males that slept less experienced higher reproductive success.
source: Similarly, male pectoral sandpipers greatly reduce their time spent sleeping during their short and intense mating season, and males that slept less actually experienced higher reproductive success (Lesku et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lesku et al., 2012.

claim: Sleep fragmentation has been shown to correlate inversely with sleep depth.
source: First, we measured the fragmentation of sleep, which has been shown to correlate inversely with sleep depth (Bastuji and García-Larrea, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bastuji and García-Larrea, 1999.

claim: Recent technological advances allowing for the use of polysomnography in field conditions have played an important role in revealing the ecological trade-offs that wild animals face when navigating decisions about when, where, and how to sleep.
source: Recent technological advances allowing for the use of polysomnography in field conditions have played an important role in revealing the ecological trade-offs that wild animals face when navigating decisions about when, where, and how to sleep (Davimes et al., 2018; Lesku et al., 2011; Lesku et al., 2012; Rattenborg et al., 2008; Rattenborg et al., 2016; Scriba et al., 2013; Voirin et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Accelerometry can introduce biases in sleep monitoring, typically by overestimating total sleep time as a result of an inability to distinguish resting wakefulness from sleep.
source: We note that the use of accelerometry can introduce biases in sleep monitoring, typically by overestimating total sleep time as a result of an inability to distinguish resting wakefulness from sleep (Ancoli-Israel et al., 2003; de Souza et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ancoli-Israel et al., 2003 and de Souza et al., 2003.

claim: Accelerometry is limited in its ability to differentiate the stages of sleep.
source: Accelerometry is also limited in its ability to differentiate the stages of sleep (Conradt et al., 1997, but see Devine et al., 2020; Winnebeck et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Gregarious animals often invest substantially in building and maintaining social relationships with their group-mates.
source: Gregarious animals often invest substantially in building and maintaining social relationships with their group-mates (Ward and Webster, 2016), and these bonds can prove essential to their fitness (Cameron et al., 2009; Campos et al., 2020; Frère et al., 2010; Riehl and Strong, 2018; Silk et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Social bonds can prove essential to the fitness of gregarious animals.
source: Gregarious animals often invest substantially in building and maintaining social relationships with their group-mates (Ward and Webster, 2016), and these bonds can prove essential to their fitness (Cameron et al., 2009; Campos et al., 2020; Frère et al., 2010; Riehl and Strong, 2018; Silk et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Animals have limited time to devote to maintaining their social bonds during the day.
source: Because animals have limited time to devote to maintaining their social bonds during the day (Dunbar, 1992), they may actively sacrifice sleep in order to invest in these relationships at night.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dunbar, 1992.

claim: At least one individual in the group was awake for 394 ± 11 min (82% ± 2%) from 21:00 to 05:00.
source: In our study, at least one individual in the group was awake for 394 ± 11 min (82% ± 2%) from 21:00 to 05:00, although each individual was only awake for 79 ± 1 min (16% ± 0.2%) of the same period.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Each individual baboon was only awake for 79 ± 1 min (16% ± 0.2%) from 21:00 to 05:00.
source: In our study, at least one individual in the group was awake for 394 ± 11 min (82% ± 2%) from 21:00 to 05:00, although each individual was only awake for 79 ± 1 min (16% ± 0.2%) of the same period.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Samson et al., 2017 found high levels of collective vigilance during the night in a group of Hadza hunter-gatherers.
source: Samson et al., 2017 found high levels of collective vigilance during the night in a group of Hadza hunter-gatherers, and they suggest that this collective vigilance may facilitate higher-intensity sleep (Samson and Nunn, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Samson et al., 2017 and Samson and Nunn, 2015.

claim: Previous research found age differences in sleep patterns linked to physiological demands during the development of the central nervous system.
source: This contrasts with previous research that found age differences in sleep patterns linked to physiological demands during the development of the central nervous system (Amlaner et al., 2009) and sex differences in sleep tied to the influence of sex steroids (Mong and Cusmano, 2016), with younger individuals sleeping more than older individuals (Knutson, 2014; Ohayon et al., 2004; Olds et al., 2010; Steinmeyer et al., 2010; Stuber et al., 2015) and females sleeping more than males in birds and humans (Lendrem, 1983; Mong and Cusmano, 2016; Roehrs et al., 2006; Steinmeyer et al., 2010; Stuber et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Previous research found sex differences in sleep tied to the influence of sex steroids.
source: This contrasts with previous research that found age differences in sleep patterns linked to physiological demands during the development of the central nervous system (Amlaner et al., 2009) and sex differences in sleep tied to the influence of sex steroids (Mong and Cusmano, 2016), with younger individuals sleeping more than older individuals (Knutson, 2014; Ohayon et al., 2004; Olds et al., 2010; Steinmeyer et al., 2010; Stuber et al., 2015) and females sleeping more than males in birds and humans (Lendrem, 1983; Mong and Cusmano, 2016; Roehrs et al., 2006; Steinmeyer et al., 2010; Stuber et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mong and Cusmano, 2016.

claim: Younger individuals sleep more than older individuals according to previous research.
source: This contrasts with previous research that found age differences in sleep patterns linked to physiological demands during the development of the central nervous system (Amlaner et al., 2009) and sex differences in sleep tied to the influence of sex steroids (Mong and Cusmano, 2016), with younger individuals sleeping more than older individuals (Knutson, 2014; Ohayon et al., 2004; Olds et al., 2010; Steinmeyer et al., 2010; Stuber et al., 2015) and females sleeping more than males in birds and humans (Lendrem, 1983; Mong and Cusmano, 2016; Roehrs et al., 2006; Steinmeyer et al., 2010; Stuber et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Females sleep more than males in birds and humans according to previous research.
source: This contrasts with previous research that found age differences in sleep patterns linked to physiological demands during the development of the central nervous system (Amlaner et al., 2009) and sex differences in sleep tied to the influence of sex steroids (Mong and Cusmano, 2016), with younger individuals sleeping more than older individuals (Knutson, 2014; Ohayon et al., 2004; Olds et al., 2010; Steinmeyer et al., 2010; Stuber et al., 2015) and females sleeping more than males in birds and humans (Lendrem, 1983; Mong and Cusmano, 2016; Roehrs et al., 2006; Steinmeyer et al., 2010; Stuber et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Baboon groups are structured by linear dominance hierarchies that shape the priority of access to resources.
source: Baboon groups are structured by linear dominance hierarchies that shape the priority of access to resources (Cheney and Seyfarth, 2008; King et al., 2009; Marshall et al., 2015), and individuals can leverage their affiliative and kinship relationships to obtain resources that they would not be able to access based on social rank alone (Sick et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cheney and Seyfarth, 2008, King et al., 2009, and Marshall et al., 2015.

claim: Baboons can leverage their affiliative and kinship relationships to obtain resources that they would not be able to access based on social rank alone.
source: Baboon groups are structured by linear dominance hierarchies that shape the priority of access to resources (Cheney and Seyfarth, 2008; King et al., 2009; Marshall et al., 2015), and individuals can leverage their affiliative and kinship relationships to obtain resources that they would not be able to access based on social rank alone (Sick et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sick et al., 2014.

claim: Early hominins were extremely vulnerable to nighttime predation in their dry savannah habitats.
source: Evidence suggests that, like baboons, early hominins were extremely vulnerable to nighttime predation in their dry savannah habitats (Brain, 1983; Treves and Palmqvist, 2007; Wrangham and Carmody, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Brain, 1983, Treves and Palmqvist, 2007, and Wrangham and Carmody, 2010.

claim: Hominins likely remained vulnerable to nocturnal predation until they began to manipulate fire.
source: Hominins likely remained vulnerable to nocturnal predation until they began to manipulate fire, around which they could sleep to reduce the risk of predation (Samson and Nunn, 2015), and some characteristics of our sleep today may be best explained in light of the vulnerability that sleep imparted on our ancestors.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Samson and Nunn, 2015.

claim: Modern humans exhibit decreased sleep quality when sleeping in an unfamiliar environment.
source: For example, modern humans exhibit decreased sleep quality when sleeping in an unfamiliar environment (Tamaki et al., 2016), similar to the baboons in our study.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tamaki et al., 2016.

claim: The lower quality sleep resulting from the 'first night effect' is limited to the first night in a new location.
source: The lower quality sleep resulting from this aptly named 'first night effect' is limited to the first night in a new location (Tamaki et al., 2016), and our findings suggest that the first night effect may be conserved from an environment where this first night would have been accompanied by poor information about risk, and thus, a higher likelihood of predation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tamaki et al., 2016.

claim: Early hominins likely slept in groups.
source: Early hominins would have also experienced a social opportunity cost of sleep as they likely slept in groups (Samson and Nunn, 2015; Willems and van Schaik, 2017) and would have experienced constraints on the time available to maintain their social network during the day until developing the advanced cognition that enabled a more efficient use of time (Nunn and Samson, 2018; Samson and Nunn, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Samson and Nunn, 2015 and Willems and van Schaik, 2017.

claim: Modern human sleep is extremely short and intense compared to that of other primates.
source: While our sleep has likely evolved substantially from that of our earliest ancestors, with modern human sleep being extremely short and intense compared to that of other primates (Nunn et al., 2016; Nunn and Samson, 2018), a full understanding of the way we sleep involves considering not only the physiological benefits of sleep, but also its ecological and social costs in the environment in which it evolved.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Nunn et al., 2016 and Nunn and Samson, 2018.

claim: The study monitored sleep and activity patterns in a group of olive baboons at Mpala Research Centre, a 200 km2 conservancy located on the Laikipia Plateau in Central Kenya.
source: We monitored sleep and activity patterns in a group of olive baboons at Mpala Research Centre (MRC), a 200 km2 conservancy located on the Laikipia Plateau in Central Kenya.
evidence: This is a description of the study location.

claim: The study trapped and anesthetized 26 individuals, which comprised more than 80% of the adults and subadults in the study group.
source: We trapped and anesthetized 26 individuals, which comprised more than 80% of the adults and subadults in the study group (see Strandburg-Peshkin et al., 2015 for details on capture methodology).
evidence: This is a description of the study methodology.

claim: The collars recorded GPS location at 1 Hz sampling interval and continuous triaxial accelerations at 12 Hz/axis from 06:00 to 18:00.
source: We fit each individual with a GPS and accelerometry collar that recorded the baboon's GPS location at 1 Hz sampling interval and continuous triaxial accelerations at 12 Hz/axis from 06:00 to 18:00.
evidence: This is a description of the study methodology.

claim: From 18:00 to 06:00, the collars recorded a 2.5 s burst of accelerations at 10 Hz/axis at the beginning of every minute.
source: From 18:00 to 06:00, the collars recorded a 2.5 s burst of accelerations at 10 Hz/axis at the beginning of every minute.
evidence: This is a description of the study methodology.

claim: The study collected 483 days of GPS data and 506 nights of accelerometry data.
source: In total, we collected 483 days of GPS data and 506 nights of accelerometry data.
evidence: This is a description of the data collected.

claim: The study adapted a well-validated sleep classification algorithm used in human research.
source: For this study, we adapted a well-validated sleep classification algorithm used in human research (van Hees et al., 2015; van Hees et al., 2018) and validated its ability to detect sleep in wild baboons.
evidence: This is a description of the study methodology, with citations to van Hees et al., 2015 and van Hees et al., 2018.

claim: The accelerometer-based sleep classification exhibited 80.7% accuracy in the validation study.
source: The validation study determined that our accelerometry-based classification of sleep exhibits 80.7% accuracy (Supplementary file 1r; see Sleep Validation Study for further details of validation study).
evidence: This is a finding from the validation study.

claim: VeDBA is a widely used measure of overall movement activity.
source: To derive metrics of sleep (sleep onset time, awakening time, total sleep time, sleep period duration, sleep efficiency, sleep fragmentation), we calculated the log of the vectorial dynamic body acceleration (VeDBA), a widely used measure of overall movement activity (Qasem et al., 2012), from 36 calendar days or 354 baboon-nights.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Qasem et al., 2012.

claim: The study used triaxial accelerometry and GPS to track the sleep patterns of a group of wild baboons over a period of a month.
source: Using triaxial accelerometry and GPS to track the sleep patterns of a group of wild baboons (Papio anubis), we found that ecological and social pressures indeed interfere with homeostatic sleep regulation.
evidence: This is a description of the study methodology.

claim: The study leveraged naturally occurring sleep disturbances to test how recent sleep history influenced arousal threshold during sleep.
source: We also leveraged naturally occurring sleep disturbances to test how recent sleep history influenced arousal threshold during sleep.
evidence: This is a description of the study methodology.
